fields.expected: I'd want to work on infrastructure for scientific research and evaluation. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded, selected, and judged, reading through the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the NIH/NSF project-grant model to newer structures like DARPA, ARPA-H, and Focused Research Organizations, and talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and science-policy people. I started out thinking grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. Talking to researchers changed that: I now think the bigger effect is selection, since people learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and never attempt the ones that aren't. The question I care about now is that AI is making generation cheap (literature search, analysis, alternative specifications, hypothesis generation) while evaluation stays scarce, because reviewer time and domain expertise don't scale. I'd want to build the technical side of that: provenance, reproducibility, methodological validation, evidence tracing, and escalation to human experts. I got interested in this concretely at Intelehealth, where I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard and found that generating an answer was much easier than deciding whether to trust it.

fields.expected: The hardest has been the machine-learning core of the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus. I own large parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. The modeling side is temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches, with anomaly scoring on top. The genuinely hard part wasn't getting a model to flag unusual sequences. It was that a detector with good offline numbers can still be useless, because an anomaly system that fires too often just replaces one problem with another. That pushed me into building a learning-to-rank layer for prioritizing alerts, and then a retrieval-augmented LLM explanation layer so an analyst can see why something surfaced rather than getting an opaque score. Getting the explanation layer to stay tied to retrieved evidence instead of producing plausible narration was its own problem. What I took from it is that for this kind of system, the interface between the model output and the human decision is as much of an engineering problem as the model, and versioning, failure modes, and documentation are part of that.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We tracked him to Garland Hall, could see him through the locked front doors, and knocked until someone let us in long enough for us to pitch ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I lead technically. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Johns Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it less because it worked and more because of what it corrected in me. I had been treating the product as mostly an engineering problem: build the passive sleep estimation, ship the app, get the pilot running. Actually making something real turned out to depend just as much on recruiting users, getting institutional buy-in, and being willing to explain out loud, repeatedly and to people who did not ask, why the thing should exist. Knocking on a locked door is a small thing, but it's the moment I stopped assuming good technical work would find its own audience.

fields.expected: The Software Engineer role resonates more, which is why I'm applying to Infrastructure. The work I've enjoyed most has been building the parts of a system that everything else depends on and that have to behave correctly under conditions nobody is watching. On my job-application agent, the interesting problems were not the browser interactions but the invariants: I used SQLite as the single source of truth because automation gets dangerous the moment application state can diverge across processes, put every application through an explicit state machine instead of ad hoc mutation, and put every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags that never default on and are never enabled in tests. I also built a validation ladder from unit to fixture to live read-only to live mutation, so a capability isn't called working just because it passes against a local fixture. At SAC Nexus I've owned the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, and a versioned FastAPI service behind the detection API. I like FDE-style problems and I've done a lot of user-facing product work, but the piece I keep gravitating back to is the durable substrate underneath, where correctness and failure modes are the whole job.
